flashcards.back: The distribution of a statistic, such as the sample mean, over many repeated samples of the same size: the sample means cluster around the true mean, with standard deviation sigma / root n.
A procedure that states a null hypothesis H0 and an alternative H1, then rejects H0 when the observed data would be sufficiently surprising if H0 were true.
The probability, computed assuming H0 is true, of getting data at least as extreme as the data observed: if H0 were true, a p-value of 0.03 means 3% of experiments would give data this extreme.
The threshold alpha, often 0.05, fixed before the test: reject H0 when the p-value is smaller than alpha. Alpha also caps the probability of a Type I error.
Rejecting a true null hypothesis - a false alarm. Its probability is alpha, the significance level chosen in advance.
Accepting a false null hypothesis - a missed signal. Its probability is beta, and the power of the test, 1 - beta, is the chance of avoiding it.

The p-value is read as a probability about the hypothesis itself. The p-value is about the data given the null: if H0 were true, 3% of experiments would give data this extreme. The p-value is computed in the world where H0 is true, so it measures the data's surprise in that world - repeating the test 100 times under H0, about 3 repeats give data this extreme. It never assigns a probability to H0 itself.

items.answer: A Type I error rejects a true null: declaring the machine miscalibrated when it is actually fine. A Type II error accepts a false null: passing the machine when it is actually miscalibrated. Alpha caps the probability of a Type I error.
